title: Lake camps, picnic bands and bands playing on the gallery
summary: He remembers lakefront camps with bands every day, his cousin killed by the lake train, bands playing on the gallery before dances, and pianos only in the red-light district.

story.theme_name: Dance halls, lake camps and riverboat bandstands
story.community_name: Dance halls, lake resorts and where bands played

blocks.x: Anything else you remember around in there or later on? Later on? Yeah, they had a lot of things happen. Well, you see a millen boy. Gee, that was New Orleans. New Orleans was New Orleans at that time. You see, modern times, I mean, it changed everything. They had a lot of camps. Just like they have now in some parts of Littlewood. You know, out on the lake, the camp's out on the lake. Well, that's... It was flooded out there with camps. And people had picnics every day. Every day. And when they had a picnic, they had a band. And you'd hear a band. And this camp, and across the way, you hear another band. I mean, you'd look over there and see who was playing. Who was in that band? Well, some of the band was an organized band. And a lot of bands would just get-together bands. But it was good. You know, they knew what they was doing. You know, they knew the tunes. They had a beat. Did you go out there when you were young? Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. I went out there. I had a cousin that got killed by Smoke and Mirror. Smoke and Mirror was that old train used to run there. Run about five miles an hour. That was on Lidgetfield Street, which is Lidgetfield still there. And it was from Swampland in those days. And this boy was hopping on and hopping off. And he fell under the wheels and got killed. His name was Rogers. And when I was a young kid at that time, my grandmother used to give a lot of picnics at the lake. And they all used to have a good time. Everybody had a good time. All the time. They had so many camps. It was just New Orleans. New Orleans no more. I mean, it's a nice city. I mean, it's a beautiful city. But I'm speaking about the fun part of it. The fun part, everybody enjoyed themselves those days. I mean, many bands, they had all types of bands. They had colored bands, white bands. It was marvelous. All good bands. They had Christian's band. I think, I don't know if it was Emile Christian's brother or Emile himself had a band. Christian band. They played at the Lidgetfield and Dauphine a lot. They used to play on the gallery out there before they would go in. At that time, most of the band would play a couple of numbers on the gallery. You see, on the gallery before they would go inside, see, to let the people know that the band was there, you see. You mean out on the little porch around the gallery? Yeah, yeah. A little porch, yeah. A little porch, yeah. Well, it was a flight up. Always was a flight up, you know. Same as the dance halls, you know. They had you upstairs. They didn't have you down on the platform, down on the floor where you danced at. They had you up in the ceiling there. And it was really fun to sight. And they didn't use no piano in those days, you know. They used the band, the bass and the guitar, they used the banjo. But most of them used the guitars in those days. Because the first time I played with the piano in the band it felt funny to me. That's right, I was so used to playing with the bass and banjo, I couldn't get used to that. But you see in the red light district, well, they had pianos, you know what I mean. And just like Pete Lala, 101 Ranch, a few clothes, and so many other players. Ponce's plays, Henry Ponce's plays, Rice, over there in a lot of clubs. How did the bands sit in the old days? They were all in just a straight line.
